title: Reading Atomic Habits
summary: Read a self-improvement book actively: ask before, answer while reading, and recall after, so you remember and use it.
learningObjectives: Set a purpose before you read
Turn one idea into a small action
keyTakeaways: Reading is not learning until you can recall it
Apply one idea at a time
explanation:
This guide gives you a **method**, not a summary of the book. It does not describe the book's chapters, because the exact structure is not known here, so the parts below are split by **position**.

A simple pace: read for 25 minutes, close the book, and write what you remember. Keep a note page with three headings: *What I remember*, *What I do not understand*, *One thing to try*.

blocks.title: How to work through it
before: Why am I reading this, and what do I want to change?
What do I already believe about how habits form?

parts.label: The opening third
parts.focus: What problem the author says they are solving, and the central idea.
questions: What is the main claim in one sentence?
What example convinces you most, and why?

parts.label: The middle third
questions: Which method could you try this week?
What would stop you from doing it?

parts.label: The last third
parts.focus: How the ideas combine and how to keep going.
questions: How would you explain the whole approach to a friend?

after: Close the book and write everything you remember.
Which one idea will you test, and when?
blocks.note: Split by position because the exact chapters are not known here.

commonMistakes: Reading fast to finish rather than to understand
Trying to apply every idea at once

quiz.question: What should you do right after a reading session?
options: Close the book and write what you remember
quiz.explanation: Recalling from memory strengthens it far more than rereading.

quiz.question: Why ask questions before reading?
options: To give your reading a purpose and something to look for
quiz.explanation: A purpose focuses attention on what matters to you.

quiz.question: You finished a part but cannot recall it. The best response is:
options: Write what you can, then check the gaps against the text
quiz.explanation: Attempting recall first shows the gaps, and checking afterwards fixes them.

recommendedResources.title: Make It Stick: The Science of Successful Learning
recommendedResources.searchQuery: Make It Stick Brown Roediger McDaniel
recommendedResources.whyRecommended: A well-regarded book on retrieval practice and effective study.

socraticChallenge.scenario: You read two chapters last week and remember almost nothing.
socraticChallenge.question: What would you change about how you read?
socraticChallenge.idealAnswer: Read in shorter sessions with a question in mind, close the book to write what you remember after each, and review the notes a day later.

exercises.prompt: After your next reading session, close the book and write three sentences about what you read.
exercises.answer: Success: three sentences written before you looked back at the text, then checked against it.

exercises.prompt: Pick one idea from the book and try it for a week.
exercises.answer: Success: one idea chosen, a specific time to do it, and a note of how it went.

reviewCards.prompt: What three things make reading active rather than passive?
reviewCards.answer: A question before, answering as you read, and recalling from memory after.

reviewCards.prompt: Why write what you remember before looking back at the book?
reviewCards.answer: Trying to recall strengthens memory and shows the gaps.
